name: zero-token
title: Zero Token Architecture
html:
Zero Token Architecture

“You are all having way too much fun burning way too many tokens”

Kelsey Hightower, opening “ZTA: Zero Token Architecture”, 26 Sep 2026, as quoted by Daniel Cranney, WeAreDevelopers ·

Every callInference on each run: tokens every time, a different answer each time, and a model in the trust path.
➜
Infer onceThen run the result as plain, deterministic code. Zero tokens per run.
➜
Once stays trueEvery answer carries its controls, so the kept code checks its act is still offered. The check costs nothing.

The first two in my words, from the talk’s page and Cranney’s write-up. The third is Fielding’s part.
say: Kelsey Hightower opened his talk on Zero Token Architecture with a line I won't forget: you are all having way too much fun burning way too many tokens. His point, in my words: an agent that runs inference on every call burns tokens, gets a different answer each time, and works against zero trust. Infer once. Then run the result as plain, deterministic code. Fair enough. But once has to stay true tomorrow, after the API changed. A script frozen against URLs it learned out of band either breaks, or pays tokens to learn them again. That's where Fielding comes back in: if every answer carries its controls, a kept script only has to check that the act it wants is still offered. That check is free.

deck:ref.name: rule-6
deck:ref.label: BOOKMARK
deck:ref.title: Enter with a bookmark; follow what's offered
deck:ref.summary: In brief: one URI and known media types to start; every next step chosen from what the server put in the answer.
deck:ref.quote: “A REST API should be entered with no prior knowledge beyond the initial URI (bookmark) and set of standardized media types that are appropriate for the intended audience (i.e., expected to be understood by any client that might use the API). From that point on, all application state transitions must be driven by client selection of server-provided choices that are present in the received representations or implied by the user’s manipulation of those representations. The transitions may be determined (or limited by) the client’s knowledge of media types and resource communication mechanisms, both of which may be improved on-the-fly (e.g., code-on-demand). [Failure here implies that out-of-band information is driving interaction instead of hypertext.]”
deck:ref.cite: Roy T. Fielding, “REST APIs must be hypertext-driven”

deck:ref.name: repeatability
deck:ref.label: REPEATABILITY
deck:ref.title: Repeatability: the same goal, the same result, every time
deck:ref.summary: Given the same inputs, the same outputs, call after call. Found once with a model, then replayed with none: the same steps, the same checks, the same result, until the controls really change. At the small scale it is one scenario that runs the same way every time.

deck:ref.name: resilience
deck:ref.label: RESILIENCE
deck:ref.title: Resilience: the server changes, the client doesn't break
deck:ref.summary: When the server changes, or misbehaves on purpose, the client takes the failure path the spec names, re-syncs, and goes on; a model comes back only when the controls really changed, to repair. At the small scale it is the regression suite and the gates that hold, even against the model.
